s: Q U A N T I T A T I V E
Rubin ramps through a leadership reset
NVIDIA shares fell 2.9% yesterday to $150.96, giving back an after-hours gain,
in the session after the company’s first results since Jensen Huang resigned as
CEO on 11 November. The quarter itself was strong: 1) revenue of $115.8bn
came in $6.7bn above LSEG consensus and $7.8bn above guidance, with Data
Center at $107.6bn as Vera Rubin began shipping; 2) the Q4 outlook of $130bn
(±3%) is $4.9bn above consensus, although the quarter has an extra (14th) week
and assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China; and 3) management
lifted its FY28 growth outlook to about 75% from about 70% in August, with
gross margin bottoming at 71-72% in Q4 before recovering to 72-73% in FY28.
What weighed on the shares was everything else. The board said it will not
reinstate Huang, the search for a permanent CEO (led by Heidrick & Struggles)
will not be rushed, the independent investigation is ongoing, and management is
still studying new Commerce Department export rules. Receivables rose to 64
days of sales and supply commitments to $390bn, so more of the growth now
We raise estimates (FY28E diluted EPS to $16.77 from $14.22, revenue to
$720.3bn, in line with consensus) but lower our price target to $190 from $206.
The target now rests on a three-stage DCF at a 12.7% WACC, which reflects a
5.07% 10-year Treasury yield and a 1.55 beta. At $150.96 the stock trades on
9.0x our FY28E EPS and is 37% below its October high. Our reverse DCF says
the price assumes operating margins fall to about 29% in the long run, less than
half today’s 67%, against the 40% we fade to. In our view that overstates the
damage a leadership change can do to a business whose product roadmap,
supply and customer commitments are set well into FY28. The risk is real, but
most of it lies beyond FY28, so the discount rate and the long-run margin decide
the value, not next year’s earnings. We stay Overweight with 26% upside. The
call would be wrong if hyperscalers and frontier labs slow orders for Rubin
while the CEO post is vacant, or if receivables and guarantees keep growing

NVIDIA sells the full computing platform for AI data centres:
GPUs, CPUs, networking, rack-scale systems and the CUDA
software layer. Data Center was 93% of Q3 revenue and the
company earns a 67% operating margin. Demand is not the
debate: revenue more than doubled from a year ago for a
second straight quarter, Rubin is the fastest ramp in the
company’s history, and management now expects about 75%
growth in FY28. The debate is durability. The shares price a
sharp fall in long-run margins, and the CEO vacancy, export
rules and NVIDIA’s growing role as a financier to its own
customers give that fear a story. We think the discount is too
wide for a business with this visibility and stay Overweight.

Q U A N T I T A T I V E
NVIDIA designs the computing platform on which most of the world’s AI models are
trained and served: GPUs, the Vera CPU, NVLink and Spectrum-X networking, rack-
scale systems and the CUDA software stack. Data Center revenue was $107.6bn in Q3
FY27, up 110% from a year ago, and the company converts that into a 67% operating
margin and $43.8bn of quarterly free cash flow. We rate the shares Overweight because
the price discounts a much faster erosion of those economics than the evidence
The quarter answered the demand question
Vera Rubin began shipping in Q3, and management described it as the fastest ramp in
the company’s history. Both Data Center sub-markets grew strongly: Hyperscale rose
23% sequentially to $60.1bn and AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise 18% to $47.5bn.
Supply commitments rose to $390bn from $279bn, mostly multi-year memory, which is
consistent with the ~75% FY28 growth management now expects. We model 70%
($720.3bn), the outlook given in August and in line with consensus, because the new
export rules are still being studied.
Leadership: a governance discount, not yet an operating one
Jensen Huang co-founded NVIDIA and ran it for 33 years; his resignation removes its
chief architect of strategy and its best-known salesperson. The board has appointed
CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and Harvey Jones, a director since 1993, as its first
chair. It has said Huang will not return and will consider internal and external
candidates. Nothing in the quarter or the outlook shows customer attrition, and the
roadmap through Rubin is in production. The cost of the vacancy is more likely to show
up in decisions not yet taken, such as the next architecture bets, pricing against custom
ASICs and capital allocation, than in FY28 revenue. We therefore carry it in the
discount rate and the long-run margin, not in near-term estimates.
The balance sheet is now part of the product
NVIDIA increasingly helps customers pay for its systems. Receivables reached $81.0bn
(64 days) on extended terms for large investment-grade customers. Maximum guarantee
exposure is $118bn, of which $105bn backs OpenAI’s leases at SB Energy’s Ohio
campus from FY29, and non-marketable stakes are carried at $65.5bn after a $1.8bn
impairment in Q3. None of this has cost cash yet, and contingent neocloud
commitments fell to $32bn from $36bn. It does mean a downturn would reach NVIDIA
through its balance sheet as well as its order book.
China is out of the numbers; new rules are not
Q3 included $2.4bn of licensed Hopper shipments to China, which have now stopped,
and the Q4 outlook assumes no China data-center compute revenue. The open question
is the Commerce Department’s new rule on remote access to compute in overseas data
centres, which management is still studying. Melius Research expects FY28 to be the
year sales to affected countries decline.
Our Dec-27 PT of $190 comes from a three-stage DCF (model forecasts to FY29E, a
second horizon to FY34E, then a fade to a 40% terminal EBIT margin and 3.0%
growth) at a 12.7% WACC. On the 5-year monthly beta (cost of equity 14.1%) the target
would be $173, which would make the stock Neutral.

Risks to Rating and Price Target
Leadership and governance: the CEO search, the board’s independent investigation
and congressional hearings could lead to further departures, legal or regulatory
findings, or strategic drift. A permanent CEO who is unknown to customers would
Customer concentration and the capex cycle: a handful of hyperscalers and frontier
labs account for most Data Center revenue (two direct customers held 18% and 17%
of receivables at end-October, per CNBC). A pause in their capex, for financing,
power or return-on-investment reasons, would hit revenue and margins together.
Competition: custom accelerators (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Meta MTIA,
Broadcom- and MediaTek-designed ASICs) and AMD are gaining share of
inference workloads, and could force NVIDIA to trade margin for volume faster

Balance-sheet exposure: $518bn of commitments (mostly supply), $118bn of
maximum guarantees and $32bn of contingent neocloud agreements. If OpenAI or a
neocloud defaults, NVIDIA could pay the shortfall or own data-centre capacity;
impairments on its $65.5bn of private stakes would also hit earnings.
Export controls and geopolitics: China is out of the outlook, but new rules on
remote access to compute in overseas data centres may cut sales in some countries
in FY28. Nearly all leading-edge supply depends on TSMC in Taiwan.
Gross margin: memory costs and the Rubin ramp take gross margin to 71-72% in
Q4; a slower recovery than the 72-73% guided for FY28 would cut our estimates.
Upside risks: revenue has beaten the outlook in each quarter of FY27; a resumption
of China sales, a quickly named CEO with customer credibility or a faster Rubin
ramp would all lift estimates and the multiple.
